items.new: It was a terrific, most pitiable, and maddening sight. The whale was now going head out, sending his spout before him in a continual tormented jet, while his one poor fin beat his side in an agony of fright. Now to this side, now to that, he swerved in his faltering flight. At every wave he broke, he either spasmodically sank into the sea or rolled sideways, lifting his one beating fin toward the sky. I have seen a bird with a clipped wing making frightened broken circles in the air, vainly trying to escape piratical hawks. But the bird has a voice, and with plaintive cries makes known her fear. Yet the fear of this vast dumb creature of the sea was chained up and enchanted in him. He had no voice except that choking respiration through his blowhole, and this made the sight of him unspeakably pitiable — while still, in his amazing bulk, his portcullis jaw, and his omnipotent tail, there was enough to terrify the bravest man who pitied him.

items.new: What other marvels might have been dug out of this monstrous cabinet there is no telling. But a sudden stop was put to further discoveries when the ship was dragged over sideways toward the sea to a most unusual degree, owing to the body's rapidly increasing tendency to sink. However, Starbuck, who was in charge, hung on to it to the last — hung on so stubbornly, in fact, that when at length the ship would have capsized if she had kept locking arms with the body, and the command was given to break clear, the strain upon the timber-heads to which the fluke-chains and cables were fastened was so immense that it was impossible to cast them off. Meanwhile, everything in the Pequod was tilted at an angle. To cross to the other side of the deck was like walking up the steep gabled roof of a house. The ship groaned and gasped. Many of the ivory inlays in her bulwarks and cabins were popped from their places by the unnatural dislocation. In vain, handspikes and crowbars were brought to bear upon the immovable fluke-chains to pry them loose from the timber-heads. And the whale had now settled so low that the submerged ends could not be reached at all, while every moment whole tons of weight seemed to be added to the sinking mass, and the ship seemed on the point of going over.

items.new: The central body of it is hidden in the snowy, sparkling mist that envelops it; and how can you tell for certain whether any water falls from it, when, whenever you are near enough to a whale to get a close view of his spout, he is always in a tremendous commotion, with the water cascading all around him? And if at such times you thought you really saw drops of moisture in the spout, how do you know that they are not merely condensed from its vapor? Or how do you know that they are not those very drops lying on the surface of the spout-hole fissure, which is countersunk into the top of the whale's head? For even when he is swimming tranquilly through the midday sea in a calm, with his raised hump as sun-dried as a dromedary's in the desert — even then the whale always carries a small basin of water on his head, just as under a blazing sun you will sometimes see a hollow in a rock filled up with rain.

items.new: Nor does this amazing strength at all cripple the graceful flexibility of its motions, where an infantlike ease undulates through a titanic power. On the contrary, those motions derive their most fearsome beauty from it. Real strength never impairs beauty or harmony but often bestows it. In everything impressively beautiful, strength has much to do with the magic. Take away the tied tendons that everywhere seem bursting from the marble in the carved Hercules, and its charm would be gone. When devout Eckerman lifted the linen sheet from Goethe's naked corpse, he was overwhelmed by the massive chest, which seemed like a Roman triumphal arch. When Angelo — Michelangelo — paints even God the Father in human form, notice the robustness there. And whatever they may reveal of divine love in the Son, those soft, curled, hermaphroditic Italian paintings in which his image has been most successfully embodied — so destitute of all brawniness — hint nothing of any power but the merely negative, feminine one of submission and endurance, which by all accounts form the peculiar practical virtues of his teachings.

items.new: The casual comparison in this chapter between the whale and the elephant — so far as some aspects of the tail of the one and the trunk of the other are concerned — should not suggest those two opposite organs are equal, much less the creatures they belong to. For as the mightiest elephant is only a terrier to Leviathan, so compared with Leviathan's tail, the elephant's trunk is only the stalk of a lily. The most dreadful blow from the elephant's trunk would be as the playful tap of a fan compared with the measureless crush and crash of the sperm whale's ponderous flukes, which have repeatedly hurled entire boats with all their oars and crews into the air, much as an Indian juggler tosses his balls.*

items.new: The more I consider this mighty tail, the more I deplore my inability to express it. At times there are gestures in it that, though they would well grace the hand of man, remain wholly inexplicable. In an extensive herd, so remarkable, at times, are these mystic gestures that I have heard hunters declare them akin to Freemason signs and symbols — that the whale, by these methods, was intelligently conversing with the world. Nor is that all: there are other motions of the whale's body as a whole, full of strangeness and unaccountable to his most experienced pursuer. However I dissect him, then, I only go skin deep. I do not know him, and never will. But if I cannot even understand the tail of this whale, how can I understand his head? Still less can I comprehend his face, when he has none. You shall see my back parts, my tail, he seems to say, but my face shall not be seen. But I cannot fully make out his back parts either. And hint what he will about his face — I say again he has no face.
